name: Tong (Stone) Shi
focus: Human-centered AI for urban transportation resilience

emuser.role: Product Strategy and User Experience | Project Contributions
emuser.description: Early-stage, mission-driven career-support initiative developing AI-assisted profile building and application workflows.
bullets: Helped define an experience-first career agent that connects a reusable record of a user's projects, skills, and experiences to job-specific recommendations and application materials.

Contributed to web-app and browser-extension workflow design, including Auto, Hybrid, and Manual modes, profile-completion checks, progress feedback, and manual job-description entry when extraction fails.

Developed product positioning around contextual matching and user agency; translated the team's concept into pitch narratives and interaction proposals for early-career applicants and career changers.
Contributed to product discussions on transparent matching criteria and synchronized profile information, identifying evaluation and data-consistency requirements for trustworthy AI assistance.

sop.title: Statement of Purpose
sop.subtitle: AI, accessibility, and urban transportation resilience

paragraphs: A transportation network can recover its connections while leaving some travelers without a usable journey. I want to understand that gap: how do infrastructure failures, environmental conditions, and individual mobility constraints interact to shape access during disruption, and when can AI improve the decisions that follow? For doctoral study in Canada beginning in Fall 2027, I propose to investigate accessibility-aware transportation resilience through geospatial analysis, constrained AI agents, and empirical evaluation. My aim is to develop tools that explain whose access is lost, how it recovers, and which interventions make recovery more equitable.

My preparation began with geographical information science at UC Santa Barbara and deepened through an M.S. in Civil and Environmental Engineering, with a transportation focus, at UC Berkeley. At UCSB, hydrological modeling and archaeological GIS taught me to construct spatial evidence from heterogeneous records. Managing a nine-person GIS team at the MesoAmerican Research Center also taught me to make analytical decisions explicit enough for others to reproduce. These experiences established a habit that remains central to my work: examine the assumptions behind a map before treating it as an explanation.

sections.heading: From spatial exposure to individual decisions
paragraphs: At Berkeley's Institute of Transportation Studies, I investigated emissions and socioeconomic exposure around 66 California airports. In a separate Caltrans and NEXTOR III project, I analyzed accident locations and safety-zone geometries across 259 airports. These studies sharpened my interest in the distribution of transportation burdens and in translating spatial analysis into planning evidence. At HuMNet Lab, work with Google Street View imagery and PyTorch-based urban perception modeling extended that interest to street-level experience across more than 90,000 road segments in Bogota. Together, these projects moved my attention from where infrastructure is located to how its conditions affect the people who use it.

Applied AI work then made the problem of individual representation more concrete. At Ditto, I developed location recommendations using geospatial tools, routing information, and user preferences. A geographically convenient destination could still be unsuitable once transit access or a user's constraints were considered. This experience strengthened my interest in models that distinguish an available option from a feasible and acceptable one.

sections.heading: Emuser: making context actionable
paragraphs: My work on Emuser extended this question from physical access to access to opportunity. Our team is developing a career-support tool around a reusable record of a person's experiences, rather than requiring that person to reconstruct their background for every application. I contributed to product strategy and interaction design connecting this record to job-specific assistance. The team's specifications cover different levels of automation, opportunities to review selected content, and a manual fallback when a job description cannot be extracted. Developing these workflows made me confront a recurring design problem: an AI recommendation is only useful when its representation of the person is adequate and its failure modes are manageable.

Emuser also exposed the difference between a persuasive output and a defensible evaluation. A polished application or a matching score does not establish that a system understood the user or improved an outcome. Our discussions about transparent matching criteria and the roadmap's emphasis on verified facts and outcome tracking helped clarify the standard I want to bring to transportation AI. The transferable contribution is a way of framing decisions: preserve relevant context, distinguish requirements from preferences, expose the basis for a recommendation, and let people correct it. In my PhD, I want to test whether these principles improve mobility decisions under disruption.

sections.heading: A bounded, testable doctoral agenda
paragraphs: I would begin with one urban transit-and-walking network and a defined service-disruption scenario. The first task would be to build a reproducible network representation combining service information, pedestrian connections, and accessibility attributes. Street-view analysis could help identify candidate barriers, but those attributes would require validation against reliable inventories or targeted audits. Traveler profiles would represent explicit mobility requirements and preferences informed by suitable data and participant input; demographic categories alone would not stand in for an individual's needs.

The second task would be to evaluate a constrained AI decision layer. A routing engine would generate feasible alternatives and enforce network and accessibility restrictions. An LLM could interpret stated preferences, explain trade-offs, or select among those alternatives, while unsupported recommendations would trigger a fallback. I would compare this approach with constraint-aware routing and conventional behavioral models under the same demand and disruption conditions. The central question is whether the AI component adds measurable value beyond the information and constraints already supplied to a simpler method.

Evaluation would connect individual outcomes to network recovery: completed essential trips, travel-time reliability, generalized travel cost, constraint violations, and the recovery of accessibility across traveler groups. I would examine sensitivity to missing data and profile assumptions, model variability, and computational cost. Held-out disruption cases and, where feasible, traveler or practitioner studies would help distinguish plausible explanations from credible behavioral performance. This staged design would support a defensible initial study before expansion to interacting hazards or larger networks.

sections.heading: The researcher I intend to become
paragraphs: I seek a Canadian doctoral environment that connects transportation engineering with spatial data science, human-centered AI, and collaboration with communities and practitioners. I want deeper training in behavioral modeling, experimental design, and uncertainty analysis so that my experience building systems becomes a foundation for research that can withstand comparison and replication. My intended contributions are a documented network and evaluation pipeline, evidence about when AI helps or fails, and an open-source prototype that others can examine and extend. Ultimately, I want to help cities judge recovery by whether people can reach the services and opportunities they need.

For much of my education, the obstacle was knowing how to enter a world that others already understood. I grew up in a small town in China and became the first person in my family to earn a bachelor's degree. When I began studying in the United States, I was learning an academic culture as well as a discipline: how to ask for guidance, approach research opportunities, and communicate an idea with confidence. Support from faculty and fellow students at UC Santa Barbara helped me find my footing. It also taught me that the existence of an opportunity and the ability to use it are different things.

As I gained confidence, I tried to make that transition easier for others. At UCSB's MesoAmerican Research Center, I managed a nine-person GIS team and helped international undergraduates navigate research, academic writing, and professional communication. Our work required both technical coordination and patience with people whose preparation differed. Presenting the Tikal research and receiving second place in the 2023 AAG GISS Student Honor Paper Competition gave me confidence in my ability to contribute. Mentoring showed me another form of achievement: helping a colleague become able to contribute independently.

Being struck by a car as a pedestrian later changed how I understood transportation. Recovery made studying and navigating daily life more difficult during my master's program. With support from my advisor and care providers, I continued my education and completed my degree at Berkeley. I also became more attentive to the distance between a route that exists on a map and a journey someone can actually undertake. I cannot generalize my experience to every traveler, but it changed the questions I ask and the assumptions I am willing to leave unexamined.

That perspective accompanied my research on airport emissions, safety, and urban perception. I wanted to understand how infrastructure distributes burdens and whose experience disappears when those burdens are averaged. These projects gave me analytical tools for questions that had become personally consequential. They also taught me that concern for a community is a starting point; useful work requires careful evidence and a willingness to revise an explanation.

sections.heading: Emuser: turning frustration into a shared project
paragraphs: Emuser grew from a different experience of that same distance between possibility and access. Our team recognized how much effort job seekers spend repeatedly translating their experiences into the language of a vacancy. The problem was not simply writing a stronger sentence. It was deciding which parts of a person's background mattered, retaining the context behind them, and helping that person choose a next step. I helped shape an experience-first product concept and the interactions through which users could receive assistance while retaining control over their own story.

The work exposed practical obstacles that enthusiasm alone could not solve. A workflow needed to remain usable when information was missing or extraction failed. Automation needed room for review. A small team needed a scope it could sustain. The concrete outputs of this phase were product narratives, interface and workflow specifications, and a shared direction for development. The later roadmap gave us a framework for limiting expansion and asking for evidence before adding another service. Those documents are not proof of improved employment outcomes; they are a foundation on which such outcomes can be tested.

Emuser taught me to value the less visible work of making an idea usable: articulating a requirement, finding an ambiguity, documenting a fallback, and making a decision understandable to a teammate. It also sharpened my sense of responsibility when building AI systems. If a tool misrepresents a person's experience, the person bears the consequence. In transportation, an unsuitable recommendation can likewise place the burden of a system's assumptions on the traveler. This connection strengthened my desire to pursue a PhD in which human needs shape both the model and the standard used to evaluate it.

sections.heading: What I will carry into doctoral life
paragraphs: I will enter doctoral study with experience moving between research and product development, and with an understanding that progress depends on other people. I hope to contribute as a researcher who documents decisions, welcomes criticism, and makes room for students who are still learning how academic work happens. My first-generation experience and the support I received during recovery have made asking for help, and making help accessible, part of how I work.

My long-term path is to develop AI-assisted transportation tools whose value can be assessed in the lives of the people they are intended to serve. During the PhD, I want to produce reproducible studies, accessible explanations, and software that researchers and practitioners can inspect. I also want to continue mentoring students navigating unfamiliar academic environments. The thread connecting my education, recovery, research, and Emuser is a commitment to making opportunity usable. I want my doctoral work to advance that commitment through evidence, thoughtful collaboration, and practical contributions to more resilient urban transportation.
